data.name: Eador. Imperium
data.detailed_description:
Hire heroes, build an army, prevail in battles and try to keep your empire intact in the face of grave danger.

Eador. Imperium is a new chapter in Eador series, known for its unique blend of grand strategy, turn-based tactics and RPG elements.

Story


A young wizard pursuing his revenge against the fanatics who have ruined his life. A barbarian priestess searching for a higher purpose for her people. A mercenary facing the abyss about to consume his home. A governor appointed to rule over a defiant province in times of great crisis.

Threads of their lives will weave a strange pattern, for the destiny of the Imperium is at stake.

Features


  • All new and handcrafted story campaign, bringing a fresh approach to the Eador formula.
  • New heroes, new units and unique Shard worlds offer even more strategic possibilities and unexpected challenges.
  • The ultimate Eador game: Imperium includes all original content from Masters of the Broken World (not counting the campaign).

reviews.review:
"Eador: Imperium" could be seen as either a new game or a large, well-made expansion to "Eador: Masters of the Broken World". The changes are barely noticeable at first glance, but under the hood practically everything has been rebalanced, and it plays quite differently.

I've always had a lot of respect for the "Eador" series. At first it may look like a technically cruder version of "Age of Wonders" or "Heroes of Might & Magic", but in practice it's a much more complex strategy game across nearly all of its systems. Unfortunately, that complexity also means a confusing interface and poor explanations. Sometimes you aren't even told that a particular mechanic exists. I suspect this creates an absurdly high barrier to entry. I'm sure plenty of people quit after discovering that their city has over 200 possible buildings, tied together by prerequisites, restrictions, and sometimes mutually exclusive choices.

"Imperium" tries to address this with a fairly extensive tutorial campaign covering many of its systems. It's still not enough. A game like this desperately needs an in-game encyclopedia, like those in "Civilization" or "Total War", explaining things such as "mood", "discontent" and "corruption", or showing what upgrades a particular unit might eventually get.

Despite looking much like its predecessor, "Imperium" changes plenty, from the economy to the size of battlefields. There are many new units and several new hero classes, which I particularly enjoyed. The Sorceress cannot learn spells in town; instead, when leveling up she chooses magic schools and spell levels, gaining access to all the corresponding spells. Probably the least unusual of the new heroes. The Legate is similar to the Commander, though it plays differently. The Pilot can fly with an entire army and attack from unexpected directions, but taking off and landing each cost a turn. I imagine that would be incredibly useful in multiplayer, but against the campaign AI the Pilot felt rather weak. The Lich, built around commanding undead, offers a genuinely different and interesting playstyle, though it requires a lot of crystals. Then there's the Sentinel, arguably the strongest new hero in my experience. Essentially a golem, it can't use equipment or artifacts, but it's powerful and versatile on its own, and can be built into a melee fighter, ranged attacker or spellcaster.

The developers also experimented with the campaigns. They feature different protagonists but share an overarching story that comes together in the final campaigns. Variety comes partly from forcing you to use specific hero classes and unit rosters, with artificial limits on which buildings you can construct. Many missions also have objectives beyond the usual "capture every enemy capital". One, for example, involves no building at all: you just move a hero around the map solving small local problems.

Unfortunately, the developers went overboard with timed missions, where you must achieve something within a set number of turns. A couple would have been fine, but there are far too many. I really dislike turn limits, especially in a single-player turn-based strategy.

I also like it when heroes carry over between missions along with their leveled-up armies, artifacts, and sometimes even their cities and provinces. Yet the final "Imperium" and "Epilogue" campaigns break that continuity. My guess is the developers ran out of time to balance everything and simply reset some values. It was especially disappointing to see heroes from previous campaigns return drastically weakened, with skill builds completely different from the ones I'd chosen. Why undo my progress? If balancing them was such a problem, they could have been NPCs instead. As it is, the story loses its sense of continuity.

And then there's the first "Epilogue" mission, where you have to find four Chaos Seals. Their appearance in provinces seems partly random, possibly without any guarantee that all four can actually be found. You might search everywhere and still lose. I recommend using a Steam guide written by someone who explains how they managed it. I followed their route, except where they needed three reloads to trigger the event, I needed thirty-three. A great test of patience.

The AI is another disappointment. I strongly advise against letting it handle battles automatically. It doesn't seem able to think even a few moves ahead within the same turn, or plan the order of your units' actions. It might buff a unit that won't attack that turn, or send a weak unit into an enemy's counterattack when a stronger one could have finished the enemy off safely. There's plenty of this nonsense.

Technically, the game isn't impressive either. I noticed no significant graphical improvements over "Masters of the Broken World", but in my experience it stutters and lags even more.

Worse still are the bugs. There are the usual crashes and incorrect descriptions of building bonuses, but also serious issues, such as heroes suddenly disappearing together with their entire armies and artifacts. Check your heroes every turn so you can reload before it's too late.

I've encountered some stranger bugs as well. In one province, bandits were stationed as guards. I couldn't dismiss them, so I tried killing them in battle. After every victory, they immediately returned as guards. I even fully explored the province and visited every special location to rule things out. No change.

Another time, I sent a hero to attack an enemy province. While the hero was on the way, an enemy hero captured one of my provinces along the route. A battle started and I won, but my hero ended up stuck in the now enemy-owned province, unable to move, while the province I'd originally intended to attack somehow became mine. On several other occasions heroes got stuck in provinces and couldn't do anything at all. No, it wasn't due to a magical barrier or siege.

I also never received the "Patience and persistence" achievement for playing 100 hours. Apparently the game has its own timer that doesn't count all playtime. I'd understand if it excluded time spent in the main menu, but I've spent well over 100 hours actually playing. Maybe it doesn't count windowed mode, maybe the timer resets because of technical or network issues, or maybe it only counts tactical battles and ignores the world map. Those are just guesses, but it's irritating regardless.

And finally, the biggest omission: there is no multiplayer whatsoever, not even hot seat. In a strategy game like this, playing against other people can keep you interested for years, especially when the computer opponent is so weak.

For all that, I still like "Eador: Imperium", just as I like the earlier games. Its mechanical changes do improve on "Masters of the Broken World", and I genuinely enjoyed playing it. But the flaws and unfinished parts add up. Oddly enough, "Masters of the Broken World" left me with more positive impressions, even though I spent only about a quarter as much time playing it.

I could forgive the bugs. Or the lack of multiplayer. Or the poor optimization. But all three together? I can't give it a positive review.
